---
applyTo: "src/core/harness/CliIntegration.ts, src/core/harness/CliLogMonitor.ts, src/core/harness/PtyProcessManager.ts"
---

<purpose>
Core CLI-harness runtime orchestration shared by every harness.
</purpose>

<architecture>
- `CliIntegration` is the workflow-facing entry point, but most behavior now lives in composed services created by `createServices()`. Prefer changing the smallest service (`CliPromptPreparer`, `CliExecutionRunner`, `CliTransportCoordinator`, etc.) instead of adding more branches/state to `CliIntegration`.
- Keep provider-specific behavior behind `ICliProvider`. If a change only applies to one harness, add or adjust a provider method; do not branch on harness ID inside `CliIntegration`.
- `buildCliArgs()` returns provider base args only. `CliIntegration` appends permission args, interactive notification-hook args, and headless user-hook args later in the run; providers should not duplicate that wiring inside `buildCliArgs()`.
- `execution.contextResolutionFailure` has two symmetric per-step chokepoints in two files: `CliIntegration.initializeExecutionSession` gates before `session.preparePrompt`, while `WorkflowExecutor` gates before `getIntegrationForPrompt`. Both must use the shared resolution predicate and formatter. The mode switches on diagnostic code—not stored severity or the presence of any diagnostic—because `prepared.diagnostics` is mixed with advisory codes that must not block. Secrets have a *whole-workflow* pre-step-1 `preflightWorkflowSecrets` check gated by the same setting, plus a **separate live per-step check** inside `WorkflowExecutor.resolveGrantedSecretValues` (called by `registerResolvedSecrets` and the two inline prompt/retry resolution sites) — this second one exists because a step's inline `!NAME` grant is only known once the step's own declared prompt text is parsed at execution time, so preflight's raw-prompt scan can miss it. Both checks independently honor `"warn"` vs `"fail"`; before this was added, the live check always hard-threw regardless of the setting — an unresolvable secret discovered mid-run (not caught by preflight) killed the whole workflow even with `contextResolutionFailure: "warn"`. `secret check` never reads this setting, for either check. When adding a prompt diagnostic code, decide deliberately whether it joins `CONTEXT_RESOLUTION_DIAGNOSTIC_CODES` — only "a declared reference failed to resolve" belongs there. `prompt.secret.interpolation-ignored` is the cautionary case: `${secret:NAME}` in prompt text used to throw unconditionally, which hard-failed runs whose prompts merely *documented* the syntax, so it is now an advisory that never blocks in either mode. Note `parseSecretReferences` (`SecretReferenceParser.ts`) only masks triple-backtick fenced blocks before scanning for `!NAME`, not inline single-backtick code spans — prose that quotes the syntax as `` `!NAME` `` is still parsed as a real grant attempt (now a "warn"-mode warning instead of a hard failure, but still a false positive worth knowing about).
</architecture>

<interactiveExecution>
- Interactive reuse is split across files: `CliIntegration` decides whether a PTY can be reused, while `CliExecutionRunner` performs inject mode against the existing PTY/log path. If a spawn-time property changes, retire the PTY instead of forcing reuse.
- MCP server properties are normalized after effective-prompt resolution and before spawn, so a later queued `/mcp:<server>` reference changes the normalized `mcpServers` snapshot; the existing inject-compatibility comparison must then retire the PTY and spawn with the newly attached server.
- **Retiring a PTY is a *session*-scoped decision, not an integration-scoped one.** `CliIntegration` can only see its own coordinator's single `currentPtySession`, but `WorkflowInstance` hands every incompatible prompt its own integration (spawn-identity cache keys), so the process holding the AI session a dispatch is about to `--resume` is routinely a *different* integration with its own coordinator — and harnesses reject or corrupt a resume of a session another process still has open, including an idle inject-mode TUI retained for a later step. Every spawn path therefore goes through `WorkflowContext.releaseConflictingAiSession` → `WorkflowInstance.releaseConflictingAiSession` → each candidate's `ownsLiveAiSession`/`releaseLiveAiSession`, before the spawn, and the retired terminal's tab is dropped with `TERMINAL_REMOVED` because the incoming process continues that same conversation. A new spawn path must be wired through that hook; the local `retireInteractivePty*` helpers do not cover it.
- PTY handoff is intentionally noisy internally: `CliIntegration` sets `suppressPtyExitSessionId` so expected shutdowns during mode changes do not surface as prompt failures.
- Do not remove the inject-mode focus/write timing. The `\x1b[I` focus-in sequence plus short delays before text and Enter are required for Copilot-style TUIs to accept injected input reliably.
- `ICliProvider.getInteractiveSpawnEnv()` has two independent call sites in `CliTransportCoordinator`: `executeStandaloneInteractiveProcess()` (CLI-only, non-VS Code path) and `startInteractiveProcess()` (the real VS Code PTY path, used by `PtyProcessManager.spawnPty()`). Both must merge it in — it was previously only wired into the standalone path, so the VS Code PTY path silently ran every interactive session with just `process.env` + caller-supplied hook vars, dropping Copilot's OTel export override (`buildOtelSpawnEnv()`, context-window tracking went dark with no error) and Claude's `CLAUDECODE` deletion. When adding a new provider-level interactive env override, grep both call sites — don't assume one covers the other.
</interactiveExecution>

<logAndTerminalFlow>
- `CliLogMonitor` runs parser-driven log polling and the optional notification monitor together. When a notification monitor exists, hook completion is authoritative and log completion is only for streaming/drain; preserve that priority.
- After completion or PTY exit, `CliLogMonitor` still drains late log entries. That drain is what preserves final tool events and context-window updates.
- `CliLogMonitor` calls `parser.readNewLines()` from **four unsynchronized places** — the `fs.watch` callback (`pump.watch`, whose handler is `async` and never awaited), the initial read, every catch-up read (background-work hold, completion, cancellation), and the drain loop — so overlapping invocations are normal, not exceptional. A parser whose read offset advances only *after* an `await` will therefore hand the same byte range to two callers and re-emit the whole turn, with different synthetic event IDs so nothing downstream can dedupe it. Parsers that read synchronously (offset assigned in the same tick as `statSync`/`readSync`) are safe by construction; anything using `fs.promises` must serialize itself. `AntigravityTranscriptReader.readRecords()` does this with a per-path promise chain — copy that shape rather than reintroducing async offset tracking.
- `runBackgroundWorkHold`'s `while` loop condition re-checks `parser.hasPendingBackgroundWork()` immediately on entry, before waiting for any new Stop-hook notification — so entering the hold silently consumes one `BackgroundFollowUpState` `staleStopGuardChecks` decrement with no intervening event. A provider configuring `staleStopGuardChecks: N` therefore needs an actual *N-1* further genuine Stop hooks after the one that triggered the hold before it releases on its own (the hold has no time-based release). Account for this when tuning a provider's guard count; see the Antigravity gotcha in `harness-cli-providers.instructions.md` for a case where assuming a guaranteed follow-up Stop was wrong.
- Each hold-loop iteration races the notification-file wait against `onHoldWake` — resolved as soon as `processEvent` runs while `holdingForBackgroundWork` is true, i.e. the still-active log watcher (or a catch-up read) processing one more event. This exists because a background task's completion notification can be consumed *mid-turn* (Claude: a `queued_command` attachment, not a between-turns `user` message — see the Claude gotcha below) with no intervening Stop, so the turn that actually clears `hasPendingBackgroundWork()` may never produce a *second* Stop-hook file to wake the loop. Confirmed against a real capture: a background Bash task's notification landed mid-turn, the model kept working for another ~40s, and only its own natural `end_turn` (not a further Stop) closed the pending state — without this race the hold (then capped at 10 minutes) sat until that cap even though the watcher had already observed the closing event well before that. Consequence for `staleStopGuardChecks`: `hasPendingBackgroundWork()` can now be re-checked once per log event processed during a hold, not just once per Stop-hook file, so a provider that reintroduces a nonzero guard (none does today — see above) would burn through it far faster than the "one check per real Stop" cadence the guard assumes and would need its own boundary-only signal instead of this generic per-event wake.
- The background-work hold is **deliberately unbounded while `hasPendingBackgroundWork()` is true** — only cancellation, PTY exit, a harness error notification, or `maxPromptTimeout` (default unlimited) release it. It used to have a fixed 10-minute cap measured from hold start (not reset by activity, despite being called an "idle" backstop), which committed real steps early: a silent `npm run test:harness` background run (~30 min, output redirected so even its task output file stayed empty), and a step whose model was still mid-turn after consuming both task notifications. Do not reintroduce a time-based release; a provider parser that can leave an ID pending forever (an unmatched notification kind, a stop tool that emits no notification) now hangs the step until the user cancels, so fix it in the parser. Also keep exactly **one** `monitorForCompletion` wait in flight per hold and re-arm it only after it settles: a log-event wake that starts a fresh wait leaves the old poller running, and an orphaned poller can consume (delete) the next Stop file with nobody reading its result.
- `PtyProcessManager` is the singleton for both AI and shell sessions. The `expectedController` / `controllerClientId` flow prevents multiple webviews from racing for the same terminal; keep it intact when editing terminal-start messages.
- Reconnect behavior depends on each PTY session’s `reconnectBuffer`. If output bypasses the PTY manager, reconnects and hosted-dashboard replay break.
- The dropdown "terminal still running" icon is driven by a **global** `ACTIVE_TERMINAL_WORKFLOWS` broadcast (single source: `PtyProcessManager.getWorkflowIdsWithRunningSessions()` → `WorkflowOrchestrator.getActiveTerminalWorkflowRefs()`), **not** the per-client terminal `sessions` store. A browser/hosted client only hydrates `sessions` for the workflow it is currently viewing (`replayWorkflowStateTo` replays terminals per-viewed-workflow), so the store can never tell it which *other* workflows have live terminals. The orchestrator re-broadcasts the set on every `TERMINAL_STARTED`/`TERMINAL_ENDED` (wired at the `setPtyPostMessage` chokepoint in `extension.ts`) and sends it per-client in `replayWorkflowStateTo` and the `GET_WORKFLOWS_LIST` reply. Refs carry `workingFilePath` so recent-list rows (keyed by working file path) match without prior hydration. Keep these broadcast/replay points in sync if you touch PTY lifecycle messaging.
</logAndTerminalFlow>

<cleanup>
- Workflow cleanup is two-phase: `getAdditionalCleanupFilePaths()` removes disposable provider artifacts, then `cleanupWorkspaceArtifacts()` restores provider-owned workspace files. Do not delete settings/config files early; parallel workflows may still depend on them.
- Windows shell/process quirks stay centralized in `PtyProcessManager` and `CliTransportCoordinator`; avoid duplicating shell resolution or spawn-env logic in providers.
- `PtyProcessManager.resolveShellInvocation(script, shellOverride?)` is the single source for "which shell runs this arbitrary script string, and how do I wrap it." It resolves the optional per-script override (trimmed) first, then `terminal.shellExecutable` (trimmed), then the platform auto-detected shell (`resolveWindowsShell()`/`resolveUnixShell()`), and wraps the script with the flag that shell kind needs to run a command line (`-Command` for pwsh/powershell, `-c` for bash/zsh/sh/fish/nu, `/d /s /c` plus an outer quote pair for cmd, `-e bash -lc` for wsl). Both `WorkflowInstance.spawnScriptPty` (interactive script-step PTYs) and `EndConditionEvaluator`'s file-not-found direct-command fallback (headless script steps/preconditions/end-conditions) call it, so a script's shell no longer depends on `executionMode` — before this existed, interactive steps hardcoded PowerShell/`/bin/sh` while headless inline commands fell through to Node's `shell:true` (cmd.exe on Windows), so the same script text could pass in one mode and fail with a shell-syntax error in the other, and neither path looked at `terminal.shellExecutable`. A script FILE with a known extension (`.ps1`/`.sh`/etc., in `EndConditionEvaluator.getScriptCommand()`) is unaffected — the extension already picks an unambiguous interpreter and doesn't go through this resolver. The *pure* half of that vocabulary — `resolveShellKind`/`shellDisplayName`, the per-platform `SHELL_CHOICES` catalog, and `getShellInvocationError` (the multi-line-under-cmd preflight) — lives in `src/utils/ShellCatalog.ts`, not here, because the dashboard imports it through the webview's `@root/utils` alias to build its shell picker and authoring-time warnings; anything the webview must share has to stay free of `vscode`/Node imports, so keep spawning, argv wrapping, and platform auto-detection on this side of that line.
</cleanup>
